Nonparametric Instrumental Variable Regression
through Stochastic Approximate Gradients
Caio Peixoto1, Yuri Saporito1, and Yuri Fonseca2
1School of Applied Mathematics, Getulio Vargas Foundation, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
2Decision, Risk and Operations, Columbia University, New York, United States
February 8, 2024
Abstract
This paper proposes SAGD-IV, a novel framework for conducting nonparametric instrumental variable
(NPIV) regression by employing stochastic approximate gradients to minimize the projected populational
risk. Instrumental Variables (IVs) are widely used in econometrics to address estimation problems in
the presence of unobservable confounders, and the Machine Learning community has devoted significant
effort to improving existing methods and devising new ones in the NPIV setting, which is known to be an
ill-posed linear inverse problem. We provide theoretical support for our algorithm and further exemplify
its competitive performance through empirical experiments. Furthermore, we address, with promising
results, the case of binary outcomes, which has not received as much attention from the community as its
continuous counterpart.
1 Introduction
Causal inference from observational data presents unique challenges, primarily due to the potential for
confounding variables that can affect both outcomes and variables of interest. The unconfoundedness
assumption, crucial in this context, posits that all confounding variables are observed and properly accounted
for, allowing for an unbiased estimation of causal effects. However, in many real-world scenarios, this
assumption is difficult to satisfy. When this is the case, approaches that rely on instrumental variables
(IVs) — quantities that are correlated with the variable of interest (relevance condition), do not affect the
outcome in any other way (exclusion condition) and are independent of the unobservable confounders — offer
a way to identify causal effects even when unobserved confounders exist. Moreover, as traditional parametric
models often require assumptions about the relationship between variables that may not hold in practice,
nonparametric IV (NPIV) models can adapt to the intrinsic structure of the data, allowing for a more nuanced
understanding of causal relationships.
There has been a recent boost of new algorithms applied to the NPIV estimation problem and its
theoretical properties. The challenge is that NPIV estimation is an ill-posed inverse problem (Newey and
Powell, 2003; Carrasco et al., 2007; Cavalier, 2011), and recent methods aim to incorporate developments
from predictive models, e.g., deep learning, while also accounting for the particular structure of the inverse
problem at hand.
In this work, we present a novel framework for NPIV estimation that relies on stochastic approximate
gradients, allowing it to seamlessly incorporate a variety of machine learning methods, such as those based
on Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) and deep learning. Moreover, we demonstrate, under minimal
assumptions, finite sample guarantees for the projected populational risk for both continuous and binary
responses.
1
arXiv:2402.05639v1  [stat.ML]  8 Feb 2024

1.1 Previous work
Many traditional approaches to IV estimation, like the two-stage least squares (2SLS) method, rely on linear
models for treatment estimation and counterfactual prediction functions. These approaches, while efficient
for estimating policy effects, depend on strong parametric assumptions. When the outcome is linear on the
causal function, nonparametric extensions of 2SLS attempt to tackle this ill-posed inverse problem (Newey
and Powell, 2003; Carrasco et al., 2007; Darolles et al., 2011) introducing model flexibility by utilizing linear
projections onto known basis or sieve functions (as in (Newey and Powell, 2003; Newey, 2013)) or kernel-based
estimators (as in (Hall and Horowitz, 2005; Darolles et al., 2011)). However, these traditional methods face
limitations in large, high-dimensional datasets as they are sensible to the particular choice of kernel and
number number of basis elements, see the discussion in (Hartford et al., 2017).
In order to propose a scalable method, (Hartford et al., 2017) uses deep learning models in each step of the
2SLS procedure. By imposing a latent structure on the first stage, (Liu et al., 2020) demonstrates theoretical
results for the DeepIV 2SLS. However, the proposed methodology is suitable only for the particular case
where the outcome (the dependent variable) is linear with respect to the causal function, so it cannot be
applied to the case of binary responses. On another note, (Singh et al., 2019) transforms the problem into
two stage kernel ridge regression through a kernel mean embedding of the distribution of the endogenous
covariate given the instrument.
Another stream of the literature focuses on the generalized method of Moments (GMM). In (Dikkala
et al., 2020), the authors propose a minimax formulation for the partial identification setting that can be seen
as a zero-sum game where the adversary picks moments and the modeler finds parameters to satisfy the IVs
moment conditions. In (Bennett et al., 2019), the authors propose a reformulation of the optimal weighted
GMM problem as a minimax problem. They rely on the identification assumption to demonstrate consistency
results. The minimax formulation was also explored in other works. In (Liao et al., 2020), the authors
formulate the risk minimization problem with Tikhonov regularization and demonstrate that it is equivalent
to a minimax formulation that ensures consistency even in the absence of the identification assumption and
(Bennett et al., 2023) provides faster convergence rates to the minimum norm solution.
To the best of our knowledge, most of the recent methods do not extend to the case of binary outcomes.
Traditionally, a common approach for binary outcomes is using a semi-parametric specification based on
control function (Horowitz, 2011). This allows for nonparametric estimation of the distribution of the
unobservables together with identification of the causal function’s parameters (Ahn et al., 1996; Rothe,
2009; Dong and Lewbel, 2015; Chitla et al., 2022). Here, taking an approach similar to (Centorrino and
Florens, 2021), we make mild assumptions about the distribution of the unobservables while keeping the
causal function nonparametric. While (Centorrino and Florens, 2021) proposes an estimation strategy based
on Thikhonov regularization, our method can be interpreted as a Landweber iteration, as it is based on a
variant of gradient descent applied to the populational risk.
1.2 Contributions
The main contributions of this work are:
• We propose a novel algorithm for NPIV estimation based on stochastic approximate gradients to directly
minimize the associated populational risk;
• In contrast with most recent work incorporating machine learning methods for NPIV estimation, our
framework also extends to binary outcomes;
• Under minimal assumptions, we provide explicit finite sample bounds on the projected populational
risk of our estimator for continuous and binary responses;
• We empirically verify that the performance of our algorithm is on par with other state-of-the-art NPIV
regression methods. We also show promising results for NPIV regression under a binary response.
2

The rest of the paper is structured as follows. We provide the basic setting for NPIV regression in Section 2.
In Sections 3 and 4 we detail the associated risk minimization problem and analytically compute its stochastic
gradient. Based on these results, we introduce our method in Section 5 and provide theoretical support
in Section 6. Finally, we discuss practical considerations concerning the algorithm’s implementation and
empirically study its performance relative to state-of-the-art machine learning methods for NPIV. Most proofs
are presented in Appendix A, while Appendixes B and C provide additional experiments and implementation
details.
2 Problem setup and notation
Let (Ω, A, P) be the underlying probability space, and let X be a random vector of covariates taking values
in X ⊆ RdX . We assume that the response variable Y is generated according to
Y = h⋆(X) + ε, (1)
where ε ∈ L2(Ω, A, P) and satisfies E[ε] = 0. We denote by PX the distribution of the r.v. X and assume
that the structural function h⋆ belongs to L2(X , B(X ), PX)1, which we simply denote by L2(X). This is a
Hilbert space with norm and inner product given by ∥h∥2
L2(X) = E[h(X)2] and ⟨h, g⟩L2(X) = E[h(X)g(X)].
We assume that E[ε | X] ̸= 0, that is, some covariates are endogenous. Finally, we assume the existence of a
random vector Z, taking values in Z ⊆ RdZ and satisfying
1. E[ε | Z] = 0, the exclusion restriction;
2. X ̸ ⊥ ⊥Z, i.e., Z is relevant.
This makes Z a valid instrumental variable. We define PZ and L2(Z) analogously to PX and L2(X). We
further consider the mild assumption that X and Z have a joint density denoted by pX,Z. Our goal is to
estimate h⋆ based on i.i.d. samples from the joint distribution of X, Z and Y .
As we have listed in the introduction, there are a few different approaches to estimate h⋆. We will follow
here the original one of (Newey and Powell, 2003), in which we take the expected value of Equation (1)
conditioned on Z to get
E[Y | Z] = E[h⋆(X) | Z]. (2)
This motivates us to define the conditional expectation operator P : L2(X) → L2(Z) given by
P[h](z) = E[h(X) | Z = z].
This is a bounded linear operator which satisfies ∥P∥ op ≤ 1 (the operator norm) and whose adjoint
P ∗ : L2(Z) → L2(X), that is also a bounded linear operator, is given by P ∗[g](x) = E[g(Z) | X = x].
Defining r(Z) = E[Y | Z], we can then rewrite Equation (2) as
r = P[h⋆]. (3)
This is a Fredholm integral equation of the first kind (Kress, 1989) and, as such, poses an ill-posed linear
inverse problem.
In this context, a common assumption (Darolles et al., 2011; Bennett et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2019)
made about P is compactness. We also need it here, noting that compact operators with infinite dimensional
range provide prototypical examples of ill-posed inverse problems (Carrasco et al., 2007). However, we wish
to phrase this assumption in a different, albeit equivalent (Carrasco et al., 2007), form:

3.1 Binary response
Here we outline how our methodology can be applied to binary response models. This is possible because we
are able to consider a general point-to-point loss function in Equation (4).
In the binary response model we consider, the only change we need to make to the data generating process
is the following:
Y = 1 {h⋆(X) + ε > 0} ,
that is, we observe a signal which indicates if the response was large enough. Here, X, Z and ε satisfy the
same assumptions as before. This is the same model explored in (Centorrino and Florens, 2021).
In order to use our method, we must first identify a suitable loss function ℓ. Define η = h⋆(X) − E[h⋆(X) |
Z] + ε, so that E[η | Z] = 0 and
Y = 1 {E[h⋆(X) | Z] + η > 0} .
Denoting by Fη|Z the conditional distribution function of η given Z, we find
E[Y | Z] = P [E[h⋆(X) | Z] + η > 0 | Z]
= 1 − Fη|Z(−E[h⋆(X) | Z]).
We now introduce the assumption that η is independent of Z, and has known distribution function F . This
is a somewhat restrictive assumption also made in (Centorrino and Florens, 2021). However, as far as we
know, this was the only work that addressed fully nonparametric IV regression for binary outcomes. Then,
we conclude
r(Z) = 1 − F (−P[h⋆](Z)),
and, since both sides are numbers in (0 , 1), a natural candidate for ℓ is
ℓ(y, y′) = BCE(y, 1 − F (−y′)),
where BCE is the binary cross entropy function: BCE(p, q) = −[p log q + (1 − p) log(1 − q)]. In the case of F
is the c.d.f. of a symmetric distribution, we have 1 − F (−y′) = F (y′) and the risk becomes
R(h) = E[BCE(r(Z), F(P[h](Z)))]. (7)
Whereas it is obvious that the quadratic loss satisfies Assumption 3.2, it is not clear whether the same is
true for the loss ℓ(y, y′) = BCE(y, F (y′)). Nevertheless, if F (x) = σ(x) ≜ 1/(1 + exp(−x/β)), the c.d.f. of a
logistic distribution with scale parameter β, one can verify that Assumption 3.2 holds. This loss function is
the one we will use for our experiments in the binary response setting in Section 8.

4 Gradient computation
As our strategy is based on minimizing the risk measure R, we would like to compute an analytical formula
for ∇R(h), where h ∈ L2(X), which is presented in the following proposition:
Proposition 4.1. The risk R is Fr´ echet differentiable and it’s gradient satisfies
∇R(h) = P ∗[∂2ℓ(r(·), P[h](·))], (8)
where P ∗ : L2(Z) → L2(X) is the adjoint of the operator P.
Remark 4.2 (Y versus r(Z)). Based on Equation (3), one should compute the risk as in Equation (4). However,
most works on NPIV (Newey and Powell, 2003; Singh et al., 2019; Muandet et al., 2020) compare P[h](Z)
directly with Y , instead of r(Z), since both these risk measures differ by a constant quantity under the
quadratic loss. One might think that considering Y instead of r(Z) in our formulation would lead to an
algorithm that does not need to estimate r(Z). Nevertheless, as shown in Appendix D, the gradients of the
risk measure under both formulations are the same.
The reader should notice that we do not have access to the operator P ∗ and one possible alternative is to
estimate it directly, as was done in (Darolles et al., 2011). However, we are able to rewrite the right hand
side of Equation (8) and obtain a stochastic gradient for R.
Corollary 4.3. The gradient of the populational risk satisfies
∇R(h)(x) = E[Φ(x, Z)∂2ℓ(r(Z), P[h](Z))], (9)

7 On computing bP,bΦ andbr
Algorithm 1 is purposefully agnostic to how the estimators bP,bΦ andbr are obtained, in order to provide the
practitioner with sufficient modeling flexibility. In what follows, we will explain the options we considered for
accomplishing these tasks in the experiments section.
Ratio of Densities. Density ratio estimation is a well studied problem in Machine Learning, with (Sugiyama
et al., 2012) being a good resource for acquainting oneself with relevant algorithms. The approaches we
follow here consist on obtaining an estimator bΦ that minimizes the (empirical version of the) quantity

obtained through the Unconstrained Least Squares Importance Fitting (uLSIF) framework described in
(Sugiyama et al., 2012) and also a neural network trained to minimize the same objective over its parameters. By

Conditional expectation operator. This is the most complex object we must estimate, since it encom-
passes all possible regressions of functions of X over Z. Not many options exist for this task, with a popular
one (Darolles et al., 2011; Carrasco et al., 2007) being the use of Nadaraya-Watson kernels (Nadaraya, 1964;
Watson, 1964). We, however, chose to employ the estimation method used as a first stage in KIV (Singh et al.,
2019), which transforms the problem into vector-valued RKHS ridge regression, due to its straightforward
implementation.

Conditional mean of Y given Z. This, in contrast, is the simplest unknown in our formulation, being
the regression function of Y over Z. We again consider two options for this task: the first is to employ the
method previously discussed in order to estimate the conditional expectation operator of Y given Z, and
then apply it to the identity function. The second option is to train a general purpose regressor, such as a
neural network.
Considering these options, we decide to specify two variants of SAGD-IV based on how they compute bΦ
andbr: Kernel SAGD-IV uses RKHS methods for both estimators, while Deep SAGD-IV employs neural
network estimators in these two tasks. The method for computing bP is KIV’s first stage in both variants.
Details are presented in Appendix C.
8 Numerical experiments
In this section, we compare the performance of the two variants of SAGD-IV explained in previous section,
Kernel SAGD-IV and Deep SAGD-IV, with that of three other notable frameworks 5 for estimating h⋆ in the
context of continuous responses:
• KIV: Since the original implementation was only publicly available in Matlab, to facilitate reproducibility
of our results we re-implemented this method in Python. This was done following the guidelines presented
in the paper’s text, as well as the validation procedure presented in Appendix A.5.2 to choose both
regularization parameters.
• DeepGMM: We used the publicly available Python implementation 6.
• DeepIV: We used the implementation available as part of the EconML package (Battocchi et al., 2019).
Hyperparameters and other implementation details are discussed in Appendix C.
We also empirically analyze our method’s inferences in a binary response setting. Unfortunately none of
the above alternatives can deal with a binary response without non trivial modifications. Furthermore, the
method proposed in (Centorrino and Florens, 2021) is not straightforward to implement and the code is not
publicly available. Hence, we do not make comparisons for this scenario.
Remark 8.1 (Sample size) . All three baseline methods we are considering need a single dataset ( X, Z, Y ) to
fit their estimator (hyperpameter validation included), whereas our method needs one dataset of ( X, Z, Y )
triplets to compute bΦ,br and br, and one dataset of Z samples to conduct the SAGD loop. To make fair
comparisons, we trained each method using the same total amount of random variable samples . For
example, DeepGMM might use 800 triplets ( X, Z, Y ) for training and 200 triplets for validation, whereas
SAGD-IV may use 600 triplets for fitting the preliminary estimators and then 1200 samples of Z for the
SAGD loop, both totaling 3000 random variable samples used to adjust the model. More details regarding
sample splitting can be found in Appendix C.

expectations. A possible justification could be the necessarily large sample size needed by the proposed
architectures. This further exemplifies our method’s robustness to limited data.
8.1.1 Stronger instrument
In (Bakhitov and Singh, 2022), the authors consider a DGP very similar to the one presented in Section 8.1,
with a slight difference: the endogenous covariate is generated as X = Z1+Z2+ϵ+γ, instead of X = Z1+ϵ+γ.
Hence, the instrumental variable Z is more correlated with X. In the IV literature this is referred to as
Z being a stronger instrument (Keane and Neal, 2023) for X, which is supposed to improve two stages
procedures by enhancing the quality of the first stage estimation. We repeat the same experiment design
presented here using this new DGP, and report the results in Figure 5 in Appendix B. To ease the comparison,
we put the results for both DGPs side by by side.

9 Conclusion
In this work, we proposed SAGD-IV, a flexible framework for performing nonparametric instrumental variable
regression, which seamlessly compasses both continuous and binary response settings. Under minimal
assumptions, we provided bounds on the risk minimization problem that our method addresses and showed
that this is translated into a strongly competitive empirical performance through several experiments.
Furthermore, by leveraging recent advances in the NPIV literature, we were able to integrate both kernel and
neural networks methods into a single estimator, which outperformed existing deep learning approaches.
Broader impact
This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning applied to IV estimation.
There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none which we feel must be specifically highlighted
here.

C Implementation details
In this section, we give practical guidelines for implementing SAGD-IV, as well further details regarding the
baseline methods.
C.1 SAGD-IV
Since the final estimator in Algorithm 1 is an average over the whole path of estimates produced by the
SAGD loop, we can improve upon its quality by discarding the first K estimatesbh1, . . . ,bhK, where K must
be chosen independently from M. In this way, it is as if we started our algorithm from bhK+1, after a warm
up period.
Regarding sample splitting, our theoretical results do not specify an optimal ratio between the M SAGD
iterations and the N samples of ( X, Z, Y ) used to compute bΦ,br and bP. We empirically determined that
M = 2N is a good guideline to follow, and it is the ratio we employed in Section 8. Of course, in real data
scenarios this ratio might be constrained due to limited data availability.
About hyperparameters:
• The Algorithm 1 learning rate was set to be αm = 1/
√
M for 1 ≤ m ≤ M;
• The warm up time K was set to 100;
• The set H was chosen as in Equation (5), with A set to 10. During our experiments, we found that this
parameter, aside from needing to be large enough for us to have h⋆ ∈ H, did not have any noticeable
influence on the resulting estimator.
20

• For Kernel SAGD-IV :
– We used Gaussian kernels, with lenghtscale parameter determined through the median heuristic;
– The regularization parameters for the three kernel ridge regressions were chosen through cross
validation. Since these parameters are essential for actual learning to take place, we selected the
values to be tested through an iterative procedure, described in Algorithm 2.
• For Deep SAGD-IV :
– For both networks in the roles of bΦ andbr, we used two hidden dense layers of sizes 64 and 32. In
the continuous response setting the activation function used was a ReLU, while for the binary
response one we used the sigmoid activation. For bΦ, we used dropout with rate 0 .01.
– Both networks were trained with a batch size of 512, using the Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015)
optimizer with learning rate of 0 .01, accross 1 .5 · 105/N epochs. We adopted L2 regularization in
the two estimators, with regularization parameters of 3 · 10−3 forbr and 5 · 10−3 for bΦ. We also
implemented early stopping in the two training procedures.
• We remind the reader that both SAGD-IV variants use kernel methods to compute bP.
C.2 DeepGMM
The modifications we made with respect to the original paper were the following:
• Instead of using 50% of the samples for training and 50% for validation, we adopted a train / validation
split of 80 / 20.
• We changed the batch size from 1024 to 256. This was done because we supplied the algorithm with
1000 training samples instead of the 2000 used in (Bennett et al., 2019), and hence a batch size of 1024
would not produce stochastic gradients.
C.3 DeepIV
We followed all the guidelines presented in the original paper for low dimensional settings.
C.4 KIV
We employed a 50/50 split between ( X, Z, Y ) and ( ˜X, ˜Z, ˜Y ) observations (see (Singh et al., 2019), Appendix
A.5.2). Regularization parameter candidates were also chosen using the selection method in Algorithm 2.

D Alternative risk
If instead of Equation (4) we defined the risk as
eR(h) = E[ℓ(Y, P[h](Z))],
then proceeding in exactly the same way as in the proof of Proposition 4.1, we would arrive at
DeR[h](f) = E[∂2ℓ(Y, P[h](Z)) · P[f](Z)]
As it is, this expression is not an inner product in L2(Z) since Y is not necessarily measurable with respect
to Z. However, if ∂2ℓ is linear with respect to its first argument, which is true for the quadratic and binary
cross entropy losses, we have
DeR[h](f) = E[∂2ℓ(Y, P[h](Z)) · P[f](Z)]
= E [E[∂2ℓ(Y, P[h](Z)) · P[f](Z) | Z]]
= E [∂2ℓ(E[Y | Z], P[h](Z)) · P[f](Z)]
= E [∂2ℓ(r(Z), P[h](Z)) · P[f](Z)] ,
which is the same expression obtained before. Hence, the gradient of R still depends on r(Z) and the resulting
method is the same.
